extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in mathematical logic, foundations of mathematics, and informed general readers
extracted.subtask_description: A concise encyclopedia-style exposition of Gödel's first and second incompleteness theorems, their hypotheses, proof ideas, technical conditions, examples, and consequences for formal systems and computability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective axiomatization (effectively generated)
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal system is effectively axiomatized if its set of theorems is recursively enumerable (there is an algorithm that can enumerate all theorems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Peano arithmetic and Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory (ZFC) are effectively generated. True arithmetic is consistent and complete but not recursively enumerable, so it does not satisfy this hypothesis of the incompleteness theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntactic (negation-)completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of axioms is syntactically complete if, for every statement in the language, the statement or its negation is provable from the axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the notion relevant to Gödel's first incompleteness theorem (distinguish from semantic completeness of a logic). The theorem shows that sufficiently expressive, consistent, effectively axiomatized systems cannot be syntactically complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of axioms is consistent if there is no statement such that both the statement and its negation are provable from the axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency is a basic hypothesis: the incompleteness theorems apply to consistent systems. Note that an inconsistent theory is trivially complete (principle of explosion). Peano arithmetic is believed consistent but cannot prove its own consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: ω-consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: A stronger technical consistency condition: a theory is ω-consistent if it does not prove ¬P(n) for every specific natural number n while also proving ∃n P(n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gödel's original proof assumed ω-consistency. Rosser's improvement later removed this stronger assumption, replacing it with ordinary consistency for the first incompleteness theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to represent sufficient arithmetic (contain arithmetic / encode integers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal system must be able to express a certain amount of elementary arithmetic (enough to carry out Gödel numbering and represent provability). Robinson arithmetic Q is one sufficient minimal collection of theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems that can express both addition and multiplication (or otherwise interpret enough arithmetic) meet the expressiveness requirement. Examples that fail: Presburger arithmetic (addition only) and theories like algebraically closed fields (cannot encode the integers), which therefore evade Gödel's hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gödel numbering / arithmetization of syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a mechanical encoding of statements, proofs, and syntactic objects as natural numbers (Gödel numbers), enabling metamathematical statements about provability to be turned into arithmetical statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This arithmetization makes it possible to replace 'proving a statement' with 'a number has a certain decidable property', a cornerstone of the incompleteness proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representability of provability (the Bew predicate)
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion 'there is a proof of statement S' must be expressible inside the system as a formula Bew(#(S)) (beweisbar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key property: if the system proves S then it proves Bew(#(S)). This allows the system to talk about its own proofs after arithmetization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagonal lemma / mechanism for self-reference
rubrics_metrics.description: For any sufficiently strong formal system and any formula form F(x) there is a sentence p such that the system proves p ↔ F(G(p)) (where G(p) is the Gödel number of p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma guarantees the existence of a sentence that (indirectly) asserts its own unprovability when F is chosen as the negation of Bew(x). It is the abstract formal tool that produces Gödel sentences without an explicit self-name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntactic form of the Gödel sentence (arithmetical complexity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Gödel sentence can be arranged to be an arithmetical formula at the Π1_0 level: a block of universal quantifiers followed by a quantifier-free body asserting nonexistence of a certain number with a decidable property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Via MRDP theorem the Gödel sentence can be expressed as the assertion that a particular polynomial never takes value zero on integer tuples; this clarifies the sentence's arithmetic character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of the Gödel sentence vs provability
rubrics_metrics.description: For a consistent, appropriately interpreted theory F the Gödel sentence G_F is unprovable in F; when interpreted in the standard model of arithmetic G_F is true (hence 'true but unprovable').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth of G_F is typically established by meta-analysis outside F (often formalizable in weak systems such as primitive recursive arithmetic). In some nonstandard models the Gödel sentence may be false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rosser's improvement (Rosser's trick)
rubrics_metrics.description: A refinement of Gödel's argument that removes the need for ω-consistency, showing the first incompleteness theorem holds under the weaker assumption of mere consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rosser's theorem constructs a Rosser sentence and uses a modified diagonalization argument; most modern statements of the incompleteness theorem incorporate this improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert–Bernays provability conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical conditions on the provability predicate Prov_A(#(P)) typically required to carry out the second incompleteness theorem: (1) If F proves P then F proves Prov_A(#(P)). (2) F proves Prov_A(#(P)) → Prov_A(#(Prov_A(#(P)))). (3) F proves Prov_A(#(P → Q)) ∧ Prov_A(#(P)) → Prov_A(#(Q)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peano arithmetic and all theories stronger than PA can verify these conditions; some weak systems (e.g., Robinson arithmetic) are strong enough for the first theorem but may not prove these conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressing consistency inside a system (the Cons(F) formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: One can canonically define a formula Cons(F) that expresses 'there is no natural number coding a derivation of a contradiction in F' (often formalized as 'no code of a derivation of 0=1 exists').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are subtleties: different formalizations of 'consistency' may be inequivalent inside F and some weaker/alternate formalizations may even be provable in F. The second incompleteness theorem concerns a particular canonical formalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second incompleteness theorem applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: For any consistent formal system F that contains a certain amount of arithmetic (and satisfies the technical conditions like the Hilbert–Bernays conditions), the canonical consistency statement Cons(F) is not provable in F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem is stronger than the first because it asserts a system cannot prove its own consistency. The proof formalizes the first theorem's argument inside F, yielding the unprovability of Cons(F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary about relative consistency proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: If a system F1 (meeting the technical conditions) proves the consistency of another system F2 that in turn proves the consistency of F1, then F1 cannot prove Cons(F2) without rendering F1 inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus a system cannot prove the consistency of any system that proves its consistency; this limits certain finitistic programs (e.g., Hilbert's program) for proving consistency by means formalizable in weaker systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions and boundary cases (systems not covered by Gödel's hypotheses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems that do not meet the effectiveness or expressiveness hypotheses are not subject to the incompleteness conclusions: e.g., true arithmetic (not recursively enumerable), Presburger arithmetic (cannot encode multiplication), algebraically closed fields (cannot encode integers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are also specially engineered weak systems (self-verifying theories, studied by Dan Willard) that avoid parts of the second theorem's conclusion by failing some technical condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undecidability vs independence (terminology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish the proof-theoretic meaning of 'undecidable' (a sentence neither provable nor refutable in a fixed deductive system) from the computability-theoretic meaning (a decision problem with no algorithm). 'Independent' is often used to mean 'undecidable' in the first sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of independent/undecidable mathematical statements in standard theories are given (continuum hypothesis, axiom of choice relative to ZF, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete examples of independent (undecidable) mathematical statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include the continuum hypothesis (independent of ZFC), the axiom of choice (independent of ZF), the Paris–Harrington principle and Goodstein's theorem (independent of Peano arithmetic), Kruskal's tree theorem (independent of PA), and many independence results in set theory and combinatorics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These show how incompleteness phenomena manifest in mainstream mathematics beyond the Gödel sentence itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship with computability theory (halting problem, Matiyasevich)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gödel's incompleteness theorem is closely related to results in recursion theory: e.g., proofs via computability show that a complete effective theory of arithmetic would make the halting problem decidable, a contradiction; Matiyasevich's theorem connects Diophantine equations to incompleteness by producing arithmetic statements whose unsolvability is undecidable in certain systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple computability-theoretic proofs (Kleene, Shoenfield, Hopcroft & Ullman) give alternate routes to the incompleteness conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chaitin's incompleteness theorem and information-theoretic variants
rubrics_metrics.description: In algorithmic information theory, for any system representing enough arithmetic there is a constant c such that no specific number can be proved in that system to have Kolmogorov complexity greater than c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chaitin's result gives another method of producing independent sentences (related to Berry's paradox) but typically assumes all axioms of the theory are true in the standard model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of a proof sketch for the first incompleteness theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof-by-contradiction has three essential parts: (1) arithmetization of syntax (Gödel numbering), (2) construction of a self-referential sentence via diagonalization, (3) showing that sentence is neither provable nor refutable (hence incompleteness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each of these parts has technical details (primitive recursive relations, provability encoding, diagonal lemma) that must be checked inside the chosen formal system or in a weak meta-theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical requirements for verifying provability conditions within a system
rubrics_metrics.description: To carry out the second incompleteness theorem one typically needs the system to be strong enough to represent and verify certain basic facts about proofs and arithmetic (so that the Hilbert–Bernays conditions and arithmetization steps can be formalized inside it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peano arithmetic suffices to verify these properties; some weaker systems may fail to formalize them, altering which incompleteness conclusions apply.
